Unit - 1: Molecular Spectroscopy, Phase Equilibria and Computational Chemistry

How to use this bank. Each chapter opens with the formulas and method you need, then the past ESA questions worked out in full. After that come exam-style practice questions, new question types that have not been asked yet, and quick-fire checks. Attempt them before looking: every answer is in the Answers section at the end of the chapter, numbered the same way. Numerical answers are computed from each question's own constants, so small differences from a printed key come from rounding. Chapter 7 has three timed mock papers.

Chapter 1: Rotational (Microwave) Spectroscopy

Topics T4

The rigid-rotor chapter is the most heavily examined part of Unit 1: a bond-length calculation, the moment-of-inertia derivation and a level/spectrum sketch appear almost every sitting.

Formulas to remember

εJ​=BJ(J+1) cm−1
B=8π2Ich​
I=μr02​,  μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​
ΔJ=±1,  line(J→J+1)=2B(J+1)
first line=2B,  spacing=2B
Method.
  1. Read the first line (or the spacing): B=line/2.
  2. I=h/(8π2cB) with c in cm s−1.
  3. μ in kg: amu × 1.66×10−27.
  4. r0​=I/μ​, then convert m → Å.

Derivation

Derivation: I = μr02 (asked ×4)

  1. Let masses m1​,m2​ be at distances r1​,r2​ from the centre of mass C, with r0​=r1​+r2​.
  2. Balance about C: m1​r1​=m2​r2​. Substitute r2​=r0​−r1​: m1​r1​=m2​(r0​−r1​)⇒r1​=m1​+m2​m2​r0​​ and r2​=m1​+m2​m1​r0​​.
  3. I=m1​r12​+m2​r22​=(m1​+m2​)2m1​m22​r02​+m2​m12​r02​​=(m1​+m2​)2m1​m2​(m1​+m2​)r02​​.
  4. ∴ I=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​r02​=μr02​. (Also the energy: Er​=21​Iω2=L2/2I, giving EJ​=8π2Ih2J(J+1)​.)

Past ESA questions with solutions

  1. 1.

    For a rigid-rotor heteronuclear diatomic molecule AX the first line in the pure rotational spectrum is at 21.18 cm−1. Derive an expression for the moment of inertia and calculate the moment of inertia and bond length of AX. (A = 1.008 amu, X = 35.45 amu; c=3×1010 cm s−1, π=3.14, h=6.627×10−34 J s, 1 amu =1.66×10−27 kg)

    Jun-24 · UE23 · Set 2(6 marks)

    Solution.
    1. Derivation: see Q1-D above (I = μr02).
    2. First line at 2B, so B=221.18​=10.59 cm−1.
    3. I=8π2cBh​=8(3.14)2(3×1010)(10.59)6.63×10−34​=2.64×10−47 kg m2 (used c=3×1010 cm s−1 because B is in cm−1)
    4. μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​=36.461.008×35.45​=0.9801 amu=1.63×10−27 kg.
    5. r0​=I/μ​=1.63×10−272.64×10−47​​=1.27×10−10 m=1.275 A˚.

    Answer: I=2.64×10−47 kg m2, r0​=1.27 Å

  2. 2.

    The first line in the pure rotational spectrum of HCl appears at 21.18 cm−1. Calculate the bond length. (H = 1.008, Cl = 35.45 amu; 1 amu =1.66×10−27 kg, c=3×108 m s−1, h=6.6×10−34 J s)

    Dec-23 · UE22(4 marks)

    Solution.
    1. Because c is given in m s−1, convert B to m−1 (×100) or use c=3×1010 cm s−1 — same result.
    2. First line at 2B, so B=221.18​=10.59 cm−1.
    3. I=8π2cBh​=8(3.14)2(3×1010)(10.59)6.60×10−34​=2.63×10−47 kg m2 (used c=3×1010 cm s−1 because B is in cm−1)
    4. μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​=36.461.008×35.45​=0.9801 amu=1.63×10−27 kg.
    5. r0​=I/μ​=1.63×10−272.63×10−47​​=1.27×10−10 m=1.272 A˚.

    Answer: r0​≈1.27 Å

  3. 3.

    For HBr, the rotational spectrum shows the first line at 17.19 cm−1. Calculate the bond length (rigid rotor). (H = 1.0, Br = 79.9 amu; h=6.627×10−34 J s, c=3×1010 cm s−1)

    Jul-23 · UE22 · A(4 marks)

    Solution.
    1. First line at 2B, so B=217.19​=8.595 cm−1.
    2. I=8π2cBh​=8(3.14)2(3×1010)(8.595)6.63×10−34​=3.26×10−47 kg m2 (used c=3×1010 cm s−1 because B is in cm−1)
    3. μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​=80.91.0×79.9​=0.9876 amu=1.64×10−27 kg.
    4. r0​=I/μ​=1.64×10−273.26×10−47​​=1.41×10−10 m=1.409 A˚.

    Answer: r0​≈1.41 Å

  4. 4.

    The first spectral line in the rotational spectrum of HI appears at 13.022 cm−1. Calculate the bond length. (H = 1.0, I = 126.9 amu; c=3×108 m s−1, 1 amu =1.66×10−27 kg, π=3.14, h=6.627×10−34 J s)

    Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 1(3 marks)

    Solution.
    1. First line at 2B, so B=213.022​=6.511 cm−1.
    2. I=8π2cBh​=8(3.14)2(3×1010)(6.511)6.63×10−34​=4.30×10−47 kg m2 (used c=3×1010 cm s−1 because B is in cm−1)
    3. μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​=127.91.0×126.9​=0.9922 amu=1.65×10−27 kg.
    4. r0​=I/μ​=1.65×10−274.30×10−47​​=1.62×10−10 m=1.616 A˚.

    Answer: I≈4.30×10−47 kg m2, r0​≈1.62 Å

  5. 5.

    For a rigid-rotor diatomic molecule: (i) draw the energy-level diagram up to J=5; (ii) draw the rotational spectrum; (iii) calculate the moment of inertia and the distance between two spectral lines if B=10.56 cm−1. (c=3×108 m s−1, π=3.14, h=6.625×10−34 J s)

    Jun-24 · UE23 · Set 1(6 marks)

    Solution.
    1. (i) Levels εJ​=BJ(J+1): 0, 2B, 6B, 12B, 20B, 30B for J = 0…5 — gaps grow 2B, 4B, 6B, 8B, 10B (Fig. G9).
    2. (ii) Allowed lines J→J+1 at 2B, 4B, 6B, 8B, 10B… equally spaced by 2B; intensity rises then falls (Fig. G10).
    3. (iii) I=8π2cBh​=8(3.14)2(3×1010)(10.56)6.625×10−34​=2.65×10−47 kg m2.
    4. Spacing between adjacent lines =2B=2(10.56)=21.12 cm−1.

    Answer: I=2.65×10−47 kg m2, spacing =21.12 cm−1

  6. 6.

    For a rotating diatomic molecule: (i) derive an expression for the moment of inertia I; (ii) if B=10 cm−1, give the rotational energy levels for J=0,1,2,3 in cm−1 and draw the energy-level diagram up to J=3.

    Jan · UE23A · Set 2(6 marks)

    Solution.
    1. (i) See derivation Q1-D.
    2. (ii) εJ​=10J(J+1): J=0→0; J=1→20; J=2→60; J=3→120 cm−1. Draw four horizontal lines at these heights (gaps 20, 40, 60) with ΔJ=+1 arrows.

    Answer: Levels: 0, 20, 60, 120 cm−1

  7. 7.

    For a rigid-rotor diatomic molecule draw the energy-level diagram up to J=6.

    Dec-24 · UE22(2 marks)

    Solution.εJ​=BJ(J+1): 0, 2B, 6B, 12B, 20B, 30B, 42B — see Fig. G9 (it is drawn to J = 6). Label J on each level and show gaps increasing 2B, 4B, … 12B.

    Answer: Levels 0, 2B, 6B, 12B, 20B, 30B, 42B

  8. 8.

    (ii) If the rotational transition J=0→1 for HCl occurs at 20.68 cm−1, find the energy required for the J=20→21 transition in cm−1. (iii) If the moment of inertia of HBr is 3.26×10−47 kg m2, at what wavenumber (in m−1) does the first line appear? (h=6.62×10−34 J s, c=3×108 m s−1)

    Jul-23 · UE22 · B(6 marks)

    Solution.
    1. (ii) J=0→1 gives 2B=20.68, so B=10.34 cm−1. Δε(J→J+1)=2B(J+1); for J=20: 2B×21=21×20.68=434.28 cm−1.
    2. (iii) B=8π2Ich​=8π2(3.26×10−47)(3×108)6.62×10−34​=857.3 m−1 (c in m s−1 gives m−1 directly).
    3. First line =2B=1715 m−1 =17.15 cm−1.

    Answer: (ii) 434.28 cm−1 · (iii) ≈ 1715 m−1

  9. 9.

    For HBr, with bond length 1.404 Å, at what energy (in m−1) does the first line appear in the rotational spectrum? (H = 1.008, Br = 79.9 amu; 1 amu =1.66×10−27 kg, c=3×108 m s−1, h=6.6×10−34 J s)

    Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 2(6 marks)

    Solution.
    1. μ=80.9081.008×79.9​ amu=0.9954 amu =1.65×10−27 kg.
    2. I=μr02​=1.65×10−27×(1.404×10−10)2=3.26×10−47 kg m2.
    3. B=8π2Ich​=855.4 m−1.
    4. First line =2B=1711 m−1 (≈ 17.11 cm−1).

    Answer: First line ≈ 1711 m−1

    How many rotational lines lie between 0 and 200 cm−1 for HI (B=6.51 cm−1)?

Quick-fire checks and spot the error

True or false

Answer first; the key explains why.

  1. 74.

    The first line in a rigid-rotor spectrum appears at B.

  2. 75.

    Adjacent lines in the rotational spectrum are separated by 2B.

  3. 76.

    A molecule must have a permanent dipole to absorb microwave radiation.

  4. 77.

    J can start at 1.

  5. 78.

    CO2 shows a pure rotational spectrum.

  6. 79.

    I=μr02​ where μ is reduced mass.

  7. 80.

    Increasing the reduced mass shifts rotational lines to higher wavenumber.

  8. 81.

    The energy gap between levels J and J+1 is 2B(J+1).

  9. 82.

    ΔJ = ±2 is the selection rule for the rigid rotor.

  10. 83.

    The most intense line is always the first line.

  11. 84.

    H2 and HD both show microwave spectra.

  12. 85.

    Rotational energy levels get closer together as J increases.

Spot the error

Each worked 'solution' contains one mistake.

  6. 91.

Selection rules and active molecules

  1. 68.

  5. 72.

Chapter 2: Vibrational (IR) Spectroscopy — Harmonic Oscillator

Topics T5

Every paper has a k ↔ ν̄ calculation, usually with zero-point energy, plus the 'why only one line' reason. Learn the one-line formula and practise the unit handling.

Formulas to remember

νˉosc​=2πc1​μk​​ cm−1
k=4π2c2νˉ2μ
εv​=(v+21​)νˉosc​
ZPE=ε0​=21​νˉosc​  (E0​=21​hcνˉ)
Δv=±1 ⇒ one line at νˉosc​
Method.
  1. Find μ in kg.
  2. νˉ=2πc1​k/μ​ (c in cm s−1 → cm−1).
  3. ZPE =21​νˉ (multiply by hc for joules).
  4. For k: k=4π2c2νˉ2μ.

Past ESA questions with solutions

  1. 1.

    (i) The force constant of HF (SHO) is 970 N m−1. Calculate the oscillation frequency (cm−1) and the zero-point energy. (ii) Why does the SHO spectrum show only one line? (c = 3×108 m s−1, π = 3.14, 1 amu = 1.66×10−27 kg; H = 1.008, F = 18.99 amu)

    Jun-24 · UE23 · Set 1(6 marks)

    Solution.
    1. μ=19.9981.008×18.99​=0.9572 amu =1.59×10−27 kg.
    2. νˉ=2πc1​μk​​=2(3.14)(3×1010)1​1.59×10−27970​​=4147 cm−1.
    3. ZPE =21​νˉ=2074 cm−1 =4.12×10−20 J (×hc).
    4. (ii) Levels εv​=(v+21​)νˉ are equally spaced and the selection rule is Δv=±1, so every allowed transition needs the same energy νˉ — one line.

    Answer: νˉ≈4147 cm−1, ZPE ≈ 2074 cm−1 ≈ 4.12×10−20 J

  2. 2.

    Same HF question with H = 1.004 amu, F = 18.998 amu (k = 970 N m−1): (i) oscillation frequency in cm−1; (ii) zero-point energy; (iii) why one line?

    Dec-24 · UE22(6 marks)

    Solution.
    1. μ=20.0021.004×18.998​=0.9536 amu =1.58×10−27 kg.
    2. νˉ=2πc1​μk​​=2(3.14)(3×1010)1​1.58×10−27970​​=4155 cm−1.
    3. ZPE =21​νˉ=2077 cm−1 =4.13×10−20 J (×hc).
    4. (iii) Equal spacing + Δv=±1.

    Answer: νˉ≈4155 cm−1; ZPE ≈ 2077 cm−1

  3. 3.

    (i) CO absorbs at 2168 cm−1 in a vibrational transition. Calculate the ground-state vibrational energy and force constant (SHO). (c=3×1010 cm s−1, h=6.625×10−34 J s, C = 12, O = 15.999 amu). (ii) Write a note on the failure of the SHO model.

    Jun-24 · UE23 · Set 2(6 marks)

    Solution.
    1. Ground state (v=0): ε0​=21​(2168)=1084 cm−1 =1084×hc=2.15×10−20 J.
    2. μ=6.8570 amu; k=4π2c2νˉ2μ=1.90×103≈1899 N m−1.
    3. (ii) See Q3 and the note after this chapter: real bonds dissociate, levels converge, overtones/hot bands occur — SHO predicts none.

    Answer: ε0​=1084 cm−1; k≈1899 N m−1

  4. 4.

    (i) Radiation absorbed by CO in a vibrational transition is 2168 cm−1. Calculate the ground-state vibrational energy and the force constant (SHO; π = 3.14, h = 6.627×10−34 J s, c = 3×1010 cm s−1, C = 12, O = 15.999). (ii) Only one peak is observed in the SHO model. Substantiate.

    Jan · UE23A · Set 2(6 marks)

    Solution.
    1. Same as the previous CO question: ε0​=1084 cm−1; k≈1.90×103 N m−1.
    2. (ii) Equal level spacing and Δv=±1.

    Answer: ZPE 1084 cm−1; k ≈ 1.90×103 N m−1

  5. 5.

    Jul-23 · UE22 · B(4 marks)

    Solution.
    1. μ=6.8570 amu =1.14×10−26 kg; νˉ=2050 cm−1=205000 m−1.
    2. k=4π2c2νˉ2μ=1.70×103 N m−1.

    Answer: k≈1700 N m−1

  6. 6.

    Solution.
    1. μ is given — no need to compute it.

    Dec-24 · UE23(4 marks)

    1. μ=27.99912.0×15.9994​=6.8570 amu =1.14×10−26 kg.
    2. νˉ=2πc1​μk​​=2(3.14)(3×1010)1​1.14×10−261840​​=2133 cm−1.

    Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 1(7 marks)

    Solution.
    1. μ=3014×16​=7.4667 amu =1.24×10−26 kg.
    2. νˉ=2πc1​μk​​=2(3.14)(3×1010)1​1.24×10−261530​​=1865 cm−1.
    3. ZPE =21​νˉ=932 cm−1 =1.85×10−20 J (using h=6.627×10−34).
    4. (ii) Equally spaced levels (gap νˉ) on a parabola; one line at νˉ (Fig. G13).
    5. (iii) ε3​=3.5νˉ=6527 cm−1; ε4​=4.5νˉ=8392 cm−1.

    Answer: ZPE ≈ 932 cm−1; ε3 ≈ 6527, ε4 ≈ 8392 cm−1

Theory questions with model answers

  1. 9.

    Why does the SHO spectrum show only one line? (asked ×5)

    Answer: Levels εv​=(v+21​)νˉ are equally spaced; the selection rule Δv=±1 allows only neighbouring-level jumps. Every jump has the same energy νˉ, so all coincide in one line.

  2. 10.

    Why is CO2 IR-active though it has no permanent dipole? (asked ×3)

    Answer: IR activity needs a change in dipole during vibration, not a permanent dipole. CO2's symmetric stretch gives no change (inactive), but the asymmetric stretch and the bending mode do (active). It has no permanent dipole, so it is microwave-inactive.

  3. 11.

    Why is HI IR-active but H2 and I2 inactive?

    Answer: HI is heteronuclear: stretching changes its dipole moment. H2 and I2 are homonuclear: zero dipole at every bond length, so the vibration never changes it.

  4. 12.

    Write a note on the failure of the SHO model. (asked ×1, relevant ×4)

    Answer: The SHO assumes a parabolic potential and equal spacing, so it predicts a single line and never dissociation. Real bonds break when stretched (anharmonic, Morse), levels converge, Δv=±2,±3 overtones and hot bands appear, and the molecule can dissociate. The SHO therefore fails at high v and cannot explain overtones.

Chapter 3: Anharmonic Oscillator and Overtones

Topics T6

Anharmonic problems are two-equation puzzles: you are given two of fundamental / overtone / ωe / xe and must find the others. Memorise the three transition expressions.

Formulas to remember

εv​=(v+21​)ωˉe​−(v+21​)2ωˉe​xe​
0→1: ωˉe​(1−2xe​)
0→2: 2ωˉe​(1−3xe​)
0→3: 3ωˉe​(1−4xe​)
1→2 (hot): ωˉe​(1−4xe​)
Method.
  1. Write the two given transitions as two equations in ωˉe​ and xe​.
  2. Subtract: ωˉe​xe​=f−o/2; then ωˉe​=3f−o and xe​=(f−o/2)/ωˉe​.
  3. If xe​ is given instead: ωˉe​=f/(1−2xe​).

Past ESA questions with solutions

  1. 1.

    For HBr the vibrational spectrum shows the fundamental at 2559.08 cm−1 and the first overtone at 5027.54 cm−1. Calculate the anharmonicity constant (anharmonic model).

    Jul-23 · UE22 · A(4 marks)

    Solution.
    1. Fundamental: ωˉe​(1−2xe​)=2559.08. First overtone: 2ωˉe​(1−3xe​)=5027.54⇒ωˉe​(1−3xe​)=2513.77.
    2. Subtract: ωˉe​xe​=2559.08−2513.77=45.31 cm−1. Then ωˉe​=2559.08+2(45.31)=3(2559.08)−5027.54=2649.70 cm−1.
    3. xe​=45.31/2649.70=0.0171.

    Answer: xe​≈0.0171 (ωˉe​≈2649.7 cm−1)

  2. 2.

    The fundamental stretching frequency of CO is 2143 cm−1 and its anharmonicity constant is 0.01. Calculate its oscillational (equilibrium) frequency.

    Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 2(2 marks)

    Solution.
    1. ωˉe​(1−2xe​)=2143.
    2. ωˉe​=1−2(0.01)2143​=0.982143​=2186.7 cm−1.

    Answer: ωˉe​≈2186.7 cm−1

  3. 3.

    Assuming CO shows anharmonic oscillation, calculate the wavenumber of the first overtone if xe​=0.017 and the equilibrium vibrational frequency is 2050 cm−1.

    Jul-23 · UE22 · B(2 marks)

    Solution.First overtone 0→2: 2ωˉe​(1−3xe​)=2(2050)(1−3×0.017)=2(2050)(0.949).

    Answer: 3890.9 cm−1

  4. 4.

    (i) What is the selection rule for the anharmonic oscillator? What is the first overtone transition? Give its expression and explain the terms.

    Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 2(4 marks)

    Solution.
    1. Selection rule: Δv=±1,±2,±3… (gross rule: dipole must change).
    2. First overtone v=0→2: Δνˉ=2ωˉe​(1−3xe​), where ωˉe​ is the equilibrium vibrational wavenumber (cm−1) and xe​ is the small positive anharmonicity constant. It is a little less than twice the fundamental.

    Answer: 2ωˉe​(1−3xe​)

  5. 5.

    Briefly describe the Born–Oppenheimer approximation and draw the ground and excited electronic states of a diatomic molecule showing rotational and vibrational energy levels (anharmonic model).

    Dec-24 · UE23(5 marks)

    Solution.
    1. B–O: electronic, vibrational and rotational energies are independent; E=Erot​+Evib​+Eelec​ (translation negligible), with Erot​≪Evib​≪Eelec​.
    2. Diagram: two Morse curves (ground below, excited above and displaced to longer re​); levels converge towards each dissociation limit; each vibrational level carries closely spaced rotational sub-levels (Fig. G15 for the Morse shape).

    Answer: See statement + diagram

Chapter 4: Electronic Spectroscopy, Franck–Condon and Raman

Topics T1–T3, T7

Largely theory: statements, diagrams and 'what can you conclude?' questions. Franck–Condon diagrams appear in more than half of all papers.

Formulas to remember

E=Erot​+Evib​+Eelec​,  Erot​≪Evib​≪Eelec​
E=hν=hcνˉ,  νˉ=1/λ
electronic lines labelled (v′,v′′)
A=logII0​​=εcl  (Beer–Lambert; older syllabus)
Method.
  1. Franck–Condon: always draw the vertical arrow from the centre of v′′=0.
  2. Compare re′​ with re′′​: equal → (0,0) strongest; larger → (v′,0) with v′>0 strongest; much larger → continuum.

Past ESA questions with solutions

  1. 1.

    State the Franck–Condon principle. With a diagram show the electronic transitions and spectra when (i) v′′=0→v′=0 is strongest; (ii) v′′=0→v′=2 is strongest.

    Dec-24 · UE22(7 marks)

    Solution.Statement as in the theory box. (i) is case (a) of Fig. G21 (re′​=re′′​): (0,0) strongest. (ii) is case (b) (re′​>re′′​): the vertical arrow ends on v′=2, so the (2,0) line is strongest and the progression peaks there.

    Answer: Cases (a) and (b)

  2. 2.

    Justify the Franck–Condon principle by drawing the transitions and spectra when (1) the internuclear distances in ground and excited states are the same; (2) the excited-state distance is much larger.

    Jun-24 · UE23 · Set 2(4 marks)

    Solution.(1) case (a): (0,0) most intense. (2) case (c): vertical arrow above the dissociation limit → continuum (Fig. G21).

    Answer: Cases (a) and (c)

  3. 3.

    (i) What is the Franck–Condon principle? If a vibrational-electronic spectrum shows a continuum, what can one infer? (ii) Why is bulk aluminium stable whereas nano aluminium is combustible?

    Jul-23 · UE22 · B(6 marks)

    Solution.(i) Statement + dissociation (theory box). (ii) is a nano-materials question (Unit 4) — not covered here.

    Answer: Dissociation

  4. 4.

    (i) State the Born–Oppenheimer approximation. (ii) What does the appearance of a continuum in an electronic spectrum let us conclude?

    Jan–May-24 · UE22(6 marks)

    Solution.Statement and dissociation reasoning — see theory box.

    Answer: See theory box

  5. 5.

    What do you mean by Rayleigh scattering and Raman scattering? Mention the difference between Stokes and anti-Stokes lines.

    Dec-23 · UE22(4 marks)

    Solution.See theory box.

    Answer: See theory box

  6. 6.

    How is it that carbon dioxide is IR active even though it has no permanent dipole? (also Jan-24 UE22 'Why is CO2 IR active but microwave inactive?')

    Jul-23 · UE22 · B(2 marks)

    Solution.See Q2 theory box: asymmetric stretch and bend change the dipole; symmetric stretch does not.

    Answer: Dipole change, not permanent dipole

Theory questions with model answers

  1. 7.

    State the Franck–Condon principle. Draw the three cases and comment on each spectrum. (asked ×5)

    Answer: Statement: “An electronic transition takes place so rapidly that a vibrating molecule does not change its internuclear distance appreciably during the transition,” so transitions are vertical.
    (a) re′​=re′′​: vertical arrow lands on v′=0; the (0,0) line is strongest and intensity falls for (1,0), (2,0)…
    (b) re′​>re′′​: arrow lands on a higher v′ (e.g. 2); the (v′,0) line with v′>0 is strongest, so the maximum is displaced along the progression.
    (c) re′​≫re′′​: arrow lands above the dissociation limit; a few discrete lines then a continuum (Fig. G21).

  2. 8.

    The vibrational–electronic spectrum of a molecule shows a continuum. What can be inferred? (asked ×2)

    Answer: The molecule has been excited above the dissociation limit of the upper state, so it dissociates into atoms. The atoms carry away the excess energy as unquantised kinetic energy, so no discrete lines appear — a continuum. (It also implies re′​≫re′′​.)

  3. 9.

    State the Born–Oppenheimer approximation. (asked ×3)

    Answer: The total energy of a molecule is the sum of independent translational, rotational, vibrational and electronic parts; translation is negligible, so E=Erot​+Evib​+Eelec​ with Erot​≪Evib​≪Eelec​ (electronic levels are far apart, rotational levels very close).

  4. 10.

    What are Rayleigh scattering and Raman scattering? Differentiate Stokes and anti-Stokes lines. (asked ×2)

    Answer: Rayleigh: elastic scattering — scattered light has the same frequency as the incident light. Raman: inelastic scattering — frequency shifts because the molecule exchanges vibrational/rotational energy with the photon. Stokes: scattered frequency lower than incident (molecule gains energy, goes up). Anti-Stokes: higher than incident (molecule loses energy, comes down); weaker because fewer molecules start in an excited level. (Transcript-based; not on the 2026 slides.)

  5. 11.

    State the Beer–Lambert law and explain the terms. (older syllabus)

    Answer: A=log(I0​/I)=εcl: absorbance is proportional to concentration c (mol L−1) and path length l (cm); ε is the molar absorptivity (L mol−1 cm−1); I0​ and I are incident and transmitted intensities. Flag: not on current slides.

  6. 12.

    Why does the excited electronic state usually have a larger equilibrium bond length?

    Answer: An electron is promoted to an antibonding orbital (e.g. π→π*), weakening the bond, so the minimum of the upper potential curve shifts to larger r.

  7. 13.

    Why do homonuclear molecules (H2, N2) show vibration/rotation only in electronic spectra?

    Answer: They have no dipole change for IR or rotation, but all molecules can undergo electronic transitions, which carry vibrational (coarse) and rotational (fine) structure.

Born–Oppenheimer and energy scales

  1. 71.

    Answer: E_vib/E_rot ≈ 136; E_elec/E_vib ≈ 28; microwave, IR, UV respectively. Hence E_rot ≪ E_vib ≪ E_elec.

  2. 72.

    Answer: Since the three energies are independent and additive, ΔE=ΔEelec​+ΔEvib​+ΔErot​: each electronic band splits into vibrational coarse structure, and each vibrational line into rotational fine structure.

  3. 73.

    Answer: Translational levels are so closely spaced and so small that they are effectively continuous and do not appear in the spectrum.

  4. 74.

    Answer: Electrons are far lighter than nuclei, so electronic motion is much faster and electronic levels are much farther apart; nuclear motion is slow.

  5. 75.

    Answer: Only electronic spectroscopy (and Raman); N2 is inactive in microwave and IR.

Franck–Condon in words (long answer practice)

  1. 76.

    Answer: Electronic excitation takes ~10−15 s but nuclei vibrate in ~10−13 s, so r stays the same during excitation: on a PE-vs-r plot the arrow is vertical.

  2. 77.

    Answer: For v=0 the probability of finding the nuclei is maximum at the equilibrium position (centre), while for higher v it is at the turning points.

  3. 78.

    Answer: A series of lines (v′,0) from v′′=0 to successive v′; they converge because the excited-state levels converge (anharmonic), reaching the dissociation limit.

  4. 79.

    Answer: Coarse = vibrational changes accompanying the electronic transition; fine = rotational changes.

  5. 80.

    Answer: Franck–Condon overlap of nuclear wave functions governs relative intensity.

Chapter 5: Phase Rule, Water and Pb–Ag Systems

Topics T8–T12

Phase equilibria questions come in three flavours: derive the rule, count C/P/F for a system, and draw-and-label a diagram. Practise counting until it is automatic.

Formulas to remember

F=C−P+2
variables=P(C−1)+2,  constraints=C(P−1)
reduced: F=C−P+1
water: F=3−P
dTdP​=TΔVΔH​
Method.
  1. Count phases P (each solid, each immiscible liquid, all gases = 1).
  2. Count components C = species − independent reactions − composition restrictions.
  3. F=C−P+2 (or C−P+1 if pressure is fixed / condensed).
  4. F=2 bivariant, 1 univariant, 0 invariant.

Derivation

Derivation of the phase rule (asked ×3)

  1. System of C components in P phases at equilibrium. Variables: temperature, pressure and the composition of each phase.
  2. Composition of one phase needs C−1 mole fractions (they sum to 1). For P phases: P(C−1). Add T and P: total variables =P(C−1)+2.
  3. At equilibrium the chemical potential of each component is equal in every phase: μiα​=μiβ​=μiγ​=⋯ — that is (P−1) equations per component, C(P−1) constraints in all.
  4. F= variables − constraints =P(C−1)+2−C(P−1)=PC−P+2−CP+C= C−P+2.

Past ESA questions with solutions

  1. 1.

    Derive the phase rule for a system of C components and P phases in equilibrium.

    Jun-24 · UE23 · Set 1(4 marks)

    Solution.See derivation Q5-D.

    Answer: F=C−P+2

  2. 2.

    Derive the phase rule for a system of C components and P phases in equilibrium.

    Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 1(4 marks)

    Solution.See derivation Q5-D.

    Answer: F=C−P+2

  3. 3.

    (i) Define component. Give the number of phases and components for the closed system MgCO3​(s) ⇌ MgO(s) + CO2​(g). (ii) Define eutectoid and peritectic points in the Fe–C system.

    Jan · UE23A · Set 2(4 marks)

    Solution.
    1. (i) Component: the smallest number of independently variable constituents by which the composition of every phase can be expressed. Phases: MgCO3(s), MgO(s), CO2(g): P=3. Species 3 − 1 reaction = C=2 (e.g. choose MgO and CO2: MgCO3 = MgO + CO2).
    2. (ii) Eutectoid: one solid phase transforms isothermally into two other solids (austenite → ferrite + cementite, 727 °C, 0.76 wt% C). Peritectic: liquid + one solid → a new solid (liquid + δ-ferrite → austenite, 1493 °C, 0.17 wt% C). Flag: Fe–C is not in the current material; values are standard textbook figures.

    Answer: P=3, C=2

  4. 4.

    (i) Why is the phase rule F=C−P+2 for water but F=C−P+1 for the Pb–Ag system? (ii) For CaCO3​(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2​(g) in a closed container give the number of components and phases.

    Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 2(6 marks)

    Solution.
    1. (i) Water is a one-component system with T and P both variable. For Pb–Ag, C=2 so F=4−P, giving F=3 for one phase — a 3-D diagram. Pressure is therefore fixed (≈1 atm) and, since solid–liquid equilibria (condensed systems, no gas) hardly depend on pressure, the rule reduces to F=C−P+1.
    2. (ii) P=3 (CaCO3, CaO, CO2); species 3 − 1 reaction ⇒ C=2.

    Answer: (ii) P=3, C=2

  5. 5.

    (i) Draw a neat labelled phase diagram of water (areas, lines, triple point, critical point, pressure, temperature) and calculate the degree of freedom along the freezing-point curve. (ii) What is the condensed phase rule and why is it applied to the two-component Pb–Ag system?

    Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 1(6 marks)

    Solution.
    1. (i) Diagram: Fig. G22. Triple point O: 0.0098 °C, 4.58 mmHg; critical point A: 374 °C, 218 atm. Along a curve C=1,P=2: F=1−2+2=1 (univariant).
    2. (ii) F=C−P+1: used when pressure is constant and the gas phase is absent (condensed systems), as in Pb–Ag where P has little effect.

    Answer: F=1 on the freezing curve

  6. 6.

    (i) Draw a neat labelled phase diagram of the water system with areas, lines and T, P values at the triple and critical points. (ii) Which phases are in equilibrium on the metastable curve? (iii) Calculate F at the triple point.

    Jun-24 · UE23 · Set 2(6 marks)

    Solution.
    1. (i) Fig. G22.
    2. (ii) Supercooled liquid water ⇌ vapour (curve OA′, an extension of OA below the triple point).
    3. (iii) C=1,P=3: F=1−3+2=0 — invariant.

    Answer: (ii) liquid + vapour; (iii) F = 0

  7. 7.

    (i) Draw the phase diagram of water, label areas and boundaries, and calculate F in the areas, along phase boundaries and at the triple point. (ii) Using the Clausius–Clapeyron equation, discuss why the melting-point curve has a negative slope. (iii) What is the reduced phase rule and when is it used?

    Dec-24 · UE23(8 marks)

    Solution.
    1. (i) Fig. G22: areas F=3−1=2; lines F=3−2=1; triple point F=3−3=0.
    2. (ii) dTdP​=TΔVΔHfus​​. Fusion: ΔH>0; ice → water decreases volume (ΔV<0), so dP/dT<0: raising pressure lowers the melting point. The slope is steep because ∣ΔV∣ is small. (OA and OB have ΔV>0 and large, so gentle positive slopes.)
    3. (iii) F=C−P+1 — for condensed systems at constant pressure.

    Answer: F = 2, 1, 0; dP/dT < 0 because ΔV < 0

  8. 8.

    (i) Draw a neat labelled phase diagram of the lead–silver system indicating areas and lines. Give the temperature and composition at the eutectic point. (ii) For the Fe–C system mention the phases in equilibrium, temperature and wt% C at the peritectic point.

    Jun-24 · UE23 · Set 1(6 marks)

    Solution.
    1. (i) Fig. G23: Pb melts at 327 °C, Ag at 961 °C; curves AO and BO fall to the eutectic point O at 303 °C, 2.6 % Ag (97.4 % Pb); areas: liquid melt; liquid + solid Ag; liquid + solid Pb; solid Pb + solid Ag. At O: C=2,P=3,F=0.
    2. (ii) Peritectic: liquid + δ-ferrite ⇌ austenite at 1493 °C, 0.17 wt% C (flag: Fe–C not in current material).

    Answer: Eutectic: 303 °C, 2.6 % Ag

  9. 9.

    (i) Draw a neat labelled phase diagram of the CO2​ system with areas, lines, triple and critical points (T, P). (ii) What is the reduced phase rule? Why is the general Gibbs rule not applied to a two-component system? [Not on current slides]

    Jan · UE23A · Set 2(6 marks)

    Solution.
    1. (i) Like water but the solid–liquid line leans right (positive slope, since solid CO2 is denser). Triple point −56.6 °C, 5.11 atm; critical point 31.1 °C, 73 atm; at 1 atm CO2 sublimes (−78.5 °C). Flag: not in current material; standard values.
    2. (ii) For C=2, F=4−P gives F=3 when P=1, needing three axes (T,P, composition). So pressure is fixed: F=C−P+1.

    Answer: Triple −56.6 °C / 5.11 atm; critical 31.1 °C / 73 atm

Answers

Set 1: Count P, C and F

  1. 10.

    Working.single substance, three physical phases.

    Answer: P=3, C=1, F=1−3+2=0 (invariant)

  2. 11.

    Working.one substance.

    Answer: P=2, C=1, F=1−2+2=1 (univariant)

  3. 12.

    Working.3 species − 1 reaction.

    Answer: P=3, C=2, F=2−3+2=1 (univariant)

  4. 13.

    Working.3 species − 1 reaction.

    Answer: P=3, C=2, F=2−3+2=1 (univariant)

  5. 14.

    Working.gas has NH3 : HCl = 1 : 1, an extra restriction.

    Answer: P=2, C=1, F=1−2+2=1 (univariant)

  6. 15.

    Working.the 1 : 1 restriction is lost.

    Answer: P=2, C=2, F=2−2+2=2 (bivariant)

  7. 16.

    Working.NaCl and water; solid, solution, vapour.

    Answer: P=3, C=2, F=2−3+2=1 (univariant)

  8. 17.

    Working.two components; liquid, liquid, vapour.

    Answer: P=3, C=2, F=2−3+2=1 (univariant)

  9. 18.

    Working.one component, three phases.

    Answer: P=3, C=1, F=1−3+2=0 (invariant)

  10. 19.

    Working.single gas phase; composition fixed by [PCl3] = [Cl2].

    Answer: P=1, C=1, F=1−1+2=2 (bivariant)

  11. 20.

    Working.3 species − 1 reaction.

    Answer: P=1, C=2, F=2−1+2=3 (multivariant)

  12. 21.

    Working.salt and water as components; hydrate, anhydrate, vapour.

    Answer: P=3, C=2, F=2−3+2=1 (univariant)

  1. 22.

    Answer: Composition: 1; total variables: 3; constraints: 0; F=3−0=3

  2. 23.

    Answer: Composition: 2; total variables: 4; constraints: 2; F=4−2=2

  3. 24.

  5. 26.

    Answer: Composition: 8; total variables: 10; constraints: 9; F=10−9=1

    Working.F=3−P.

    Answer: Area F=2 (bivariant); line F=1 (univariant); triple point F=0 (invariant).

  2. 28.

    Answer: OA vaporisation (water ⇌ vapour); OB sublimation (ice ⇌ vapour); OC fusion (ice ⇌ water, negative slope); OA′ metastable supercooled water ⇌ vapour.

  3. 29.

    Answer: Triple point 0.0098 °C, 4.58 mmHg; critical point 374 °C, 218 atm.

  4. 30.

    Answer: The liquid–vapour interface vanishes — above the critical temperature no pressure can liquefy the vapour.

  5. 31.

    Answer: It decreases: ice melts to a smaller volume (ΔV<0), so by Clausius–Clapeyron dP/dT<0.

  6. 32.

    Answer: P=2, F=1; at fixed 1 atm T is fixed at 0 °C (normal melting point).

Set 4: Clausius–Clapeyron slopes (extension)

  1. 33.

    Working.dP/dT=ΔH/(TΔV).

    Answer: dP/dT=−1.35×107 Pa K−1≈−133 atm K−1 — large and negative: very steep curve OC.

  2. 34.

    Working.Same equation.

    Answer: dP/dT≈3567 Pa K−1 ≈ 35.2×10−3 atm K−1 — positive and tiny by comparison (large ΔV), so OA is gentle.

Set 5: Reduced phase rule and the Pb–Ag system

  1. 36.

    Working.Condensed system (no gas), pressure fixed.

    Answer: Because C=2 would need 3-D at F=C−P+2; at constant pressure one variable is removed.

  2. 37.

    Working.C=2,P=3.

    Answer: F=2−3+1=0 (invariant). Phases: solid Pb, solid Ag and liquid melt (303 °C, 2.6 % Ag).

  3. 38.

    Answer: Curves: P=2 so F=1 (univariant); liquid region P=1 so F=2 (bivariant).

  4. 39.

    Working.10 % Ag is richer in Ag than the eutectic (2.6 % Ag), so the melt cools until it meets the Ag freezing-point curve (O to the Ag melting point): solid Ag separates first and the melt becomes richer in Pb.

    Answer: Solid Ag separates first on the Ag-side curve; the melt composition slides down that curve to O (303 °C, 2.6 % Ag); there Pb and Ag crystallise together at constant temperature (halt, F = 0); below 303 °C: solid Pb + solid Ag. (A melt with less than 2.6 % Ag would separate Pb first.)

  5. 40.

    Answer: A mixture of two components with the lowest freezing point of all compositions; it has a definite composition and a sharp melting point and solidifies at constant temperature (F = 0).

  6. 41.

    Answer: At the eutectic F=0: temperature stays fixed while all three phases coexist until solidification is complete.

Set 6: Cooling curves (thermal analysis)

  1. 42.

    Answer: Smooth fall, then a halt at the freezing point (solid and liquid coexist, F=C−P+1=1−2+1=0), then a fall again. (Fig. G24)

  2. 43.

    Answer: Fall → break (change of slope) when the first solid appears (heat of crystallisation slows cooling, F=1) → fall → halt at the eutectic temperature (F=0) → fall.

  3. 44.

    Answer: Record cooling curves for several compositions; read the break and halt temperatures; plot them against composition and join the break points (liquidus) and the common halt temperature (eutectic line).

Complete the F-table

  1. 63.

    Working.C=1.

    Answer: Areas: P=1, F=2. OA, OB, OC: P=2, F=1. OA′ (metastable, liquid+vapour): P=2, F=1. Triple point O: P=3, F=0. Critical point A: liquid and vapour become identical; treated as invariant (F=0).

  2. 64.

    Working.C=2, reduced rule.

    Answer: Liquid melt: P=1, F=2. Liquid + one solid: P=2, F=1. Solid Pb + solid Ag: P=2, F=1. Curves AO and BO: P=2, F=1. Eutectic O: P=3 (Pb + Ag + melt), F=0. Pure metal melting point A or B: C=1, P=2 ⇒ F = 1−2+1 = 0.

  3. 65.

    Working.F=0.

    Answer: F = 0 (invariant): T and P are both fixed; changing either removes at least one phase.

  4. 66.

    Working.Two phases, C=1.

    Answer: F = 1 − 2 + 2 = 1; fixing the pressure at 1 atm uses up the single degree of freedom, so T is fixed at 100 °C.

  5. 67.

    Working.F≥0⇒P≤C+2.

    Answer: P_max = C + 2 = 5 (general rule); for a condensed system, P_max = C + 1.

  6. 68.

    Working.Pmax​=C+2 and C+1.

    Answer: General: 3, 4, 5, 6. Condensed: 2, 3, 4, 5 (so Pb–Ag has at most 3 phases at the eutectic).

    Answer: Plot break temperatures against composition for the liquidus curves, the common halt temperature for the eutectic line, and the pure-metal halts for the two ends (see Fig. G24).

Definitions in your own words

  1. 98.

    Answer: Homogeneous, physically distinct, mechanically separable part. Examples: a mixture of gases is one phase; two immiscible liquids (oil + water) are two phases; each polymorph (rhombic/monoclinic sulphur) is a separate phase.

  2. 99.

    Answer: Smallest number of independently variable constituents that express every phase's composition. Zero/negative coefficients let a constituent be absent from a phase or be consumed (e.g. CaO = CaCO3 − CO2).

  3. 100.

    Answer: Number of intensive variables (T, P, concentration) that can be varied independently without changing the number of phases; for liquid water alone F = 2.

  4. 101.

    Answer: A system in which the gas phase is absent, so small pressure changes have little effect (solid–liquid).

  5. 102.

    Answer: A state not at the true minimum of Gibbs energy but persisting until disturbed — supercooled water below 0 °C (curve OA′).

  6. 103.

    Answer: Heterogeneous system at equilibrium, not influenced by external forces (gravity, electrical, magnetic).

  7. 104.

    Answer: F = 2, 1, 0 respectively.

Derivation variants and logic

  1. 105.

    Answer: Pressure is held constant (condensed system), removing one variable: F=C−P+2−1=C−P+1.

  2. 106.

    Answer: F=2−1+2=3: T, P and composition must all be specified — a 3-D diagram.

  3. 107.

    Answer: In each phase the mole fractions sum to 1, so only C−1 are independent.

  4. 108.

    Answer: For each of C components, P chemical potentials must be equal: P−1 independent equations.

  5. 109.

    Answer: variables =2(2)+2=6; constraints =3; F=3 (=3−2+2).

  6. 110.

    Answer: Matter flows from higher to lower μ; at equilibrium μ is equal in all phases and there is no net transfer.

True or false

  1. 111.

    Answer: False — at constant pressure use F=C−P+1.

  2. 112.

    Answer: True — a phase is not defined by the number of pieces.

  3. 113.

    Answer: True — NH3 : HCl = 1 : 1 in the gas, so one component; C=2 if extra NH3 or HCl is added.

  4. 114.

    Answer: False — F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0.

  5. 115.

    Answer: False — negative: ΔV<0.

  6. 116.

    Answer: False — it lowers it slightly.

  7. 117.

    Answer: True — 374 °C, 218 atm.

  8. 118.

    Answer: True — solid Pb, solid Ag and melt.

  9. 119.

    Answer: False — the lowest.

  10. 120.

    Answer: False — its vapour pressure is higher.

  11. 121.

    Answer: False — components are the minimum independent set; species − reactions − restrictions.

  12. 122.

    Answer: True — gases are completely miscible.

Spot the error

  1. 123.

    Answer: Three species minus one reaction gives C = 2.

  2. 124.

    Answer: F = C − P + 2 with C = 1: 1 − 3 + 2 = 0.

  3. 125.

    Answer: Variables = P(C − 1) + 2 (mole fractions sum to 1).

  4. 126.

    Answer: Use the reduced rule: 2 − 3 + 1 = 0.

  5. 127.

    Answer: Ice is less dense (ΔV < 0 on melting), so the slope is negative.

  6. 128.

    Answer: F = 1 − 2 + 2 = 1.

Chapter 6: Computational Chemistry

Topics T13

A recently added topic: one question in 2025 so far (definition + three applications). Expect short-answer questions.

Formulas to remember

Classical: MM, MD  ∣  Quantum: semi-empirical, ab initio, DFT

Past ESA questions with solutions

  1. 1.

    (i) What is computational chemistry? Give any three applications of computational chemistry.

    Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 2(7 marks)

    Solution.
    1. Definition: a set of techniques that solves chemical problems by simulating molecular, biological or materials systems to give reliable, accurate, atomic-level information, using theoretical chemistry built into efficient computer programs.
    2. Three applications: (1) predicting molecular properties — HOMO/LUMO and UV-Vis, IR, NMR spectra; (2) studying reaction mechanisms and kinetics; (3) designing new materials (conductivity, thermal stability); (also drug discovery by simulating drug–target interaction).

    Answer: Definition + any three applications

Practice: exam-style variants

Quick-fire checks and spot the error

True or false

  1. 37.

    Molecular mechanics treats atoms as spheres and bonds as springs.

  2. 38.

    DFT calculates the full many-electron wave function.

  3. 39.

    Ab initio methods are usually faster than semi-empirical ones.

  4. 40.

  10. 46.

    Molecular dynamics is based on the laws of motion.

Spot the error

  3. 49.

    Ethylene's HOMO is π*.

Answers

Set 1: Short answers

  1. 2.

    Answer: Techniques to simulate chemical systems and compute properties at the atomic level. First theoretical work: Heitler and London, 1927.

  2. 3.

    Answer: Molecular properties/spectra, reaction mechanism and kinetics, material design, drug discovery.

  3. 4.

    Answer: Classical (molecular mechanics, molecular dynamics): Newtonian, atoms as spheres and bonds as springs, electrons ignored, very fast. Quantum (semi-empirical, ab initio, DFT): based on the Schrödinger equation, treat electrons explicitly, slower but more accurate.

  4. 5.

    Answer: Model of a molecule as balls (atoms) joined by springs (bonds), energy from classical force fields; large molecules such as steroids can be optimised in seconds.

  5. 6.

    Answer: DFT derives the electron density directly instead of a conventional many-electron wave function; faster than ab initio but slower than semi-empirical.

  6. 7.

    Answer: Speed: MM > semi-empirical > DFT > ab initio. Accuracy (generally): ab initio > DFT > semi-empirical > MM.

  7. 8.

    Answer: Easier, cheaper and safer than experiments. It does not replace experiments; it helps chemists design and develop desired products.

  8. 9.

    Answer: 1 Define geometry of C2H4; 2 select a basis set; 3 apply the method to get orbital energies and density; 4 solve the equations for the wave function / electron density; 5 visualise the orbitals (HOMO = π, LUMO = π*).

  9. 10.

    Answer: Each carbon is sp2: 2 C–H σ bonds + 1 C–C σ bond; one unhybridised p orbital per carbon forms the π bond. HOMO = π, LUMO = π*.

  10. 11.

    Answer: Scopes: accelerated molecular discovery; property prediction; reaction-pathway mapping; structure generation. Advantages: massive speed-up (hours/days → milliseconds once trained); large-scale screening; pattern recognition of structure–property relations.

Which method would you use?

  1. 12.

    Answer: Molecular mechanics — balls and springs, very fast.

  2. 13.

    Answer: Molecular dynamics — applies laws of motion to follow atom movements.

  3. 14.

    Answer: Semi-empirical — a middle road; can handle transition states and excited states.

  4. 15.

    Answer: DFT — derives electron density directly; faster than ab initio, slower than semi-empirical.

  5. 16.

    Answer: Ab initio — based on the Schrödinger equation and the wave function; the most demanding.

  6. 17.

    Answer: A quantum method (DFT or semi-empirical).

  7. 18.

    Answer: Fast classical methods (MM/MD) plus AI/ML surrogate models trained on quantum data.

  8. 19.

    Answer: MD for dynamics, DFT for electronic structure; AI to speed up screening.

Compare the methods

  1. 20.

    Answer: MM: classical, no electrons, fastest, lowest. MD: classical dynamics, no electrons, fast. Semi-empirical: quantum (approximate Schrödinger), yes, fast, medium. DFT: quantum (density), yes, medium, high. Ab initio: quantum (wave function), yes, slowest, highest.

  2. 21.

    Answer: The set of equations/parameters that gives the potential energy of a molecule as the sum of attractive and repulsive atom–atom interactions (bond stretching, bending, non-bonded).

  3. 22.

    Answer: A mathematical function from the Schrödinger equation describing electrons; ∣ψ∣2 gives the electron probability density.

  4. 23.

    Answer: The set of mathematical functions used to build molecular orbitals in a calculation (step 2 of the ethylene workflow).

  5. 24.

    Answer: Cost grows quickly with molecular size and accuracy; results depend on the chosen method/basis set and are not a replacement for experiment.

  6. 25.

    Answer: Walter Kohn and John Pople (DFT and computational methods). [Added for clarity; 2013: Karplus, Levitt, Warshel.]

Ethylene and the electronic-structure workflow

  1. 26.

    Answer: 5 σ (4 C–H + 1 C–C) and 1 π; each carbon is sp2.

  2. 27.

    Answer: π: in-phase overlap of the two p orbitals (bonding, HOMO). π*: out-of-phase overlap with a node between the carbons (antibonding, LUMO).

  3. 28.

    Answer: 1 Define geometry. 2 Select basis set. 3 Apply the method (orbital energies and density). 4 Solve equations (wave function / density). 5 Visualise (orbital diagrams, density maps, HOMO and LUMO).

  4. 29.

    Answer: Absorption of light promotes an electron HOMO → LUMO; a smaller gap absorbs at longer wavelength (see Ch. 4 N1).

  5. 30.

    Answer: Its π electrons are higher in energy and more exposed than the σ framework; the HOMO (π) donates and the LUMO (π*) accepts electrons.

  6. 31.

    Answer: It is described by torsional terms in a force field: staggered conformers lowest, eclipsed highest (Fig. G25).

AI-enhanced computational chemistry

  1. 32.

    Answer: Quantum simulations generate data → build a dataset → train an ML model → predict properties in milliseconds.

  2. 33.

    Answer: Accelerated molecular discovery; property prediction; reaction-pathway mapping; structure generation.

  3. 34.

    Answer: Massive speed-up (hours/days → milliseconds after training); broad screening of vast chemical spaces; pattern recognition of subtle structure–property relationships.

  4. 35.

    Answer: It is trained on data produced by quantum simulations (or experiments); the model interpolates, it does not replace the underlying physics.

  5. 36.

    Answer: Battery-electrolyte or polymer screening: predict stability and conductivity of thousands of candidates before synthesis.

True or false

  1. 37.

    Answer: True — classical force field.

  2. 38.

    Answer: False — it derives the electron density directly.

  3. 39.

    Answer: False — slower but more accurate.

  4. 40.

    Answer: False — it complements them.

  5. 41.

    Answer: True — slide 3.

  6. 42.

    Answer: True — slide 16.

  7. 43.

    Answer: False — classical methods ignore electrons.

  8. 44.

    Answer: True — slide 20.

  9. 45.

    Answer: True — slide 10.

  10. 46.

    Answer: True — slide 9.

Spot the error

  1. 47.

    Answer: Ab initio ('from the beginning') uses the Schrödinger equation with no empirical parameters (that is what semi-empirical methods add).

  2. 48.

    Answer: DFT is faster than ab initio but slower than semi-empirical.

  3. 49.

    Answer: HOMO is π (bonding); LUMO is π*.
